title: Yemen: 64 children killed and 64 injured as renewed fighting cuts off care and classrooms
subtitle: UNICEF’s latest warning describes an emergency extending beyond the battlefield: disrupted water supplies, inaccessible health care and hundreds of thousands of children uprooted from home.
author: ATHENA

paragraphs.text: At least 64 children have been killed and another 64 injured in Yemen since fighting escalated on 3 September, UNICEF said on 18 November. Its warning centres on densely populated areas around Taiz and Lahj, where attacks and displacement are damaging the services families need to survive.

The figures cover the renewed escalation, not a single attack or the entire war. UNICEF’s statement does not attribute each child’s death or injury to a particular party. It calls on all parties to protect children and allow safe, unimpeded humanitarian access.

The danger extends to places where people seek treatment. UNICEF said seven schools and 28 health facilities had been damaged since the escalation began. An attack on the UNICEF-supported Al-Suqyah Health Centre in Lahj on 2 November reportedly killed five people, including three health workers. Those reported deaths should not be confused with a separate count of children killed there.
A road closure becomes a household emergency

UNICEF’s detailed situation update describes the closure of the Aden–Taiz road through Al Turbah and insecurity on alternative routes. More than 800,000 people in Taiz were reportedly cut off from humanitarian assistance as of 23 October. That is a dated access estimate, not a newly verified count for 20 November.

The same update reports that water production in the city had fallen by nearly half and food and fuel prices had more than doubled. Shortages of medicines, oxygen, electricity and fuel threatened emergency services, including maternal and newborn care.

These are connected pressures. A functioning clinic needs more than a building: it needs staff, supplies, power and a route patients can use. A delivery of medicines cannot restore care if the next delivery is blocked or if families cannot safely reach the facility.

For mothers and other caregivers, protection therefore includes access to treatment and affordable essentials as well as safety from direct attack. Measuring the crisis only through deaths and injuries leaves much of that burden outside the frame.

UNICEF says more than 1,160 schools in affected areas have closed or suspended teaching, interrupting learning for more than half a million students. It also reports that roughly one in three children recently screened by its mobile teams had acute malnutrition. This is a finding among children reached for screening; it is not a representative estimate for every child in Yemen.

Local educators and aid workers are trying to preserve routines. In a report published on 23 September, the Norwegian Refugee Council described remedial teaching and psychosocial support delivered with CARE and the Nahda Makers Organization, with funding from Education Cannot Wait.

The NRC account follows Jannat, a girl learning to read and write at Al-Marhoom Jaafar School in Taiz. Her experience illustrates what a return to education can mean, without establishing that similar support is reaching all displaced children. “Education changed my life,” she told NRC.

The organisation also described committees of parents, teachers and local leaders mapping hazards around learning spaces. Their work matters because families are participants in protecting children, even while the security conditions around them remain beyond their control.
Access must last longer than one delivery

UNICEF’s situation update, citing the International Organization for Migration, records more than 330,000 people displaced between 3 September and 10 November, including an estimated 174,000 children. It seeks US$8.5 million for urgent assistance to 560,000 affected and displaced people.

The response is already reaching some families. The update records safe-water assistance for 77,817 people and health and nutrition services for 91,300. These programme totals should not be added together as a count of different people: a family may receive more than one service.

The practical test for authorities and armed parties is whether civilian routes, health facilities and aid operations can function consistently. For donors, it is whether funding arrives quickly enough to sustain those services. Neither an appeal nor an isolated convoy establishes that children now have reliable access to help.

Yemen’s children need to survive this escalation with their health, families and opportunities intact. Accountability must cover the direct violence and the decisions that make water, treatment and education unreachable.
